title: Dynamic Portfolio Optimization with Real Datasets Using Quantum Processors and Quantum-Inspired Tensor Networks
abstract_summary: This work addresses dynamic portfolio optimization on real financial data (daily prices over 8 years for 52 assets) using discrete QUBO formulations. The authors implement and compare classical solvers, D-Wave Hybrid quantum annealing, two VQE-based approaches on IBM-Q (including a novel VQE-Constrained method), and a quantum-inspired Tensor Network optimizer, using clustering preprocessing; they report that D-Wave Hybrid and Tensor Networks handle the largest problem sizes (demonstrated up to 1272 fully-connected qubits) and discuss extensions for realistic constraints and performance improvements.
methodology_description: The authors formulate the dynamic portfolio optimization problem in a discrete QUBO form by binary-encoding discrete asset allocations (ωn,t) with Nq bits per asset and including returns, covariance-based risk, transaction costs (approximated as quadratic) and Lagrange penalty terms to enforce budget constraints. They preprocess real financial data (daily prices for 52 assets over 8 years) via Hodrick–Prescott smoothing, compute log-returns, estimate covariance with a 20-business-day window, remove low-variance/low-return assets, and apply hierarchical clustering (Euclidean distance on trends) to reduce dimensionality (typically to 6–8 clusters for some solvers). They construct several benchmark dataset sizes (XS to XXL) with varying N, Nt, Nq and Ntot. Multiple solvers are applied to the resulting QUBO/HUBO problems: classical baselines (exhaustive search for small sizes and Gekko), D-Wave Hybrid quantum annealing (using problem decomposition / hybrid classical-quantum workflow), two VQE-based approaches on IBM-Q (a standard VQE with an ansatz of single-qubit y-rotations and entangling CNOT layers; and a VQE-Constrained variant that collects multiple low-energy states per time step and recombines them classically), and a quantum-inspired Tensor Network (matrix product state) optimizer using imaginary-time evolution tailored to the problem. Performance is compared across metrics including Sharpe ratio, percentual profit (returns minus transaction costs), and computational time. Key global parameters used in experiments include risk-aversion γ = 1 and transaction-cost quadratic coefficient λ = 1.
algorithms_used: Tensor Network optimization (Matrix Product State, imaginary-time evolution)
frameworks: MATLAB (used for Tensor Network implementation / runs)
experimental_setup: Real-data experiments: daily prices of 52 assets over eight years. Preprocessing: Hodrick–Prescott smoothing, log-returns, 20-business-day rolling covariance, remove low-variance/low-return assets (reduced to ≈28 relevant assets), hierarchical clustering by Euclidean distance on trends to produce cluster-level assets (typically 6–8 clusters for constrained solvers). Discrete time rebalancing once per month. Binary encoding ωn,t = (1/K) Σ_{q=0}^{Nq-1} 2^q x_{n,t,q} yields a QUBO matrix Q of size Ntot = N * Nt * Nq. Solvers applied per dataset size; VQE circuits with ~12 active qubits (ansatz: single-qubit y-rotations and layers of CNOTs; circuit stated as 82 CNOTs & 24 variational rotations in the paper). D-Wave Hybrid used for large problems (up to 1272 fully-connected logical qubits in hybrid mode). Tensor Network (MPS) optimization via imaginary-time evolution implemented and executed on a laptop (MacBook Pro) using MATLAB for timings reported.
dataset_used: Daily price time series for 52 assets (mix including government bonds, variable and fixed income securities) over 8 years. Derived log-returns per business day, aggregated to monthly-period rebalancing returns. Covariance estimated from prior 20-business-day windows. Pre-filtering removed assets with simultaneous sub-average variance and returns, reducing to ~28 relevant assets. Clustering (hierarchical with Euclidean distance on trends) used to further reduce dimensionality to 6–8 clusters for some experiments.

results_summary: The authors implemented and compared multiple classical, quantum, hybrid, and quantum-inspired solvers for the discrete dynamic portfolio optimization problem on a real dataset (52 assets, 8 years). They preprocessed the data via smoothing and clustering to reduce dimensionality for restricted hardware. Empirically, D-Wave Hybrid and a Tensor Network optimizer handled the largest instances (up to 1272 fully-connected qubits in demonstrative runs). D-Wave Hybrid produced the largest percentual profit on the largest dataset (67.6%) in short wall-clock time (171 s), while the Tensor Network solver achieved higher Sharpe ratio (15.83) but required far longer computation (authors report ~116,833 s for the XXL case on their Matlab laptop implementation). VQE (IBM-Q) was limited to small problem sizes (~12 qubits) and required clustering; the authors also developed a VQE-Constrained hybrid strategy. There was no universally best solver: relative performance depends on the metric (profit, Sharpe, runtime). The paper also discusses methods to include additional realistic constraints and proposes algorithmic/hardware improvements as future work.
performance_claims: D-Wave Hybrid solved an instance with 1272 fully-connected qubits (XXL dataset) and returned 67.6% percentual profit, completing in 171 seconds (Table III and IV).

Tensor Network solver handled the same 1272-variable instance (XXL) and reported a Sharpe ratio of 15.83 and percentual profit 39.7%, with runtime 116,833 seconds on the authors' Matlab/MacBook Pro implementation (Tables II–IV).

Gekko (classical solver) produced large percentual profits on mid-size problems (e.g., 71.6% profit for the XL dataset) and Sharpe ratios up to 20.76 (XL), but ran out of memory beyond ~500 qubits (Tables II–IV).

VQE (IBM-Q) was run up to 12 qubits (ansatz with 82 CNOTs and 24 parametrized single-qubit rotations); reported runtimes include ~278 s for the smallest XS dataset run (Table IV) and limited scalability.

The exhaustive solver could handle up to the S/M scale reported (e.g., exhaustive returned Sharpe 8.90 on S dataset); exhaustive runtimes very small for XS (0.005 s) but scale exponentially (Table IV).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not claim a definitive quantum advantage. Instead, it reports that hybrid quantum-classical (D-Wave Hybrid) and quantum-inspired (Tensor Network) approaches can handle larger instances than direct NISQ VQE on current universal hardware, and that relative performance depends on the metric (profit, Sharpe, runtime). The authors emphasize hybrid methods' practical utility rather than asserting a demonstrated quantum computational advantage over classical approaches.
limitations: VQE on current universal quantum hardware is limited to small problem sizes (up to ~12 qubits in this work) and requires problem-size reduction (clustering) to be useful.
D-Wave 2000Q native hardware embedding restricts fully-connected problems to ~65 qubits; full-size problems require hybrid decomposition (D-Wave Hybrid).
Gekko (classical solver) hits a memory wall around ~500 qubits and cannot scale to larger problem instances tested here.

The Tensor Network (TN) solver in the current implementation is computationally slow for large instances (e.g., XXL: ~1.17e5 s) even though it can handle many variables; run-time and code optimization are needed.
Transaction costs were approximated by a quadratic (parabolic) form instead of using exact linear absolute values; the approximation may introduce modeling error.
Exact linear transaction costs and some realistic constraints (e.g., 10-5-40 rule) require ancilla/qubit expansion or higher-order (HUBO) terms, which substantially increase problem complexity.

Some realistic constraints (market impact, exact transaction costs, regulatory rules) lead to non-quadratic or higher-order formulations (cubic/quartic/HUBO) that are harder to solve on current QUBO-based hardware.
Preprocessing through clustering (dimensionality reduction) is required for some solvers but may discard relevant information and affects the fidelity of the unfolded trading trajectories.
Minimizing the Hamiltonian (energy) does not necessarily maximize financial metrics such as profit or Sharpe ratio; different solutions optimize different metrics.
There is no single best algorithm or hardware platform across all figures of merit (profit, Sharpe, run-time, monetary cost): performance depends on the chosen metric.

The VQE-Constrained approach is heuristic (e.g., sampling top-10 low-energy states per time step) and relies on the assumption that the global trajectory can be built from near-optimal instantaneous states.
The market-impact model used is simple (linear form ∆ω^T Λ' ω) and may not capture complex real-world market microstructure effects.
Empirical data processing choices (e.g., Hodrick-Prescott smoothing, choice of cluster count) influence results and introduce model-selection sensitivity.
[inferred] The TN implementation reported is not yet production-grade: it lacks software/hardware optimizations (parallelization, GPUs/HPC) and algorithmic refinements.

[inferred] The study uses a limited dataset (daily prices of 52 assets over 8 years) and clustered reduction to 28 relevant assets; generalization to broader markets or higher-frequency trading is untested.

[inferred] Hybrid solver performance and scaling depend on proprietary or evolving hardware (e.g., D-Wave Hybrid, IBM-Q improvements), so repeatability and long-term benchmarking are sensitive to platform changes.

key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrates NISQ-era VQE on IBM-Q for small/clustered instances (~12 active qubits) with real-device metrics (Sharpe ratio, percent profit, runtime), showing feasibility but severe size limits.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Employs hybrid workflows: D-Wave Hybrid decomposition for large QUBOs and a VQE-Constrained hybrid (collect low-energy states on QPU and recombine classically), enabling much larger logical problem sizes (reported up to Ntot=1272).

#idea:quantum-advantage — Reports that D-Wave Hybrid can handle the largest formulated problems and provides competitive solutions on real datasets, but any claimed advantage is conditional on hybrid decomposition and problem preprocessing.

#contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — A quantum-inspired classical Tensor Network (MPS imaginary-time evolution) matches or outperforms some quantum solvers and scales to large instances on a laptop, challenging assertions of clear quantum superiority for this task.

#contradiction:scalability — Pure variational NISQ approaches (VQE) do not scale beyond very small clustered problems, while hybrid annealing and classical TN methods scale—paper thus presents mixed/contradictory evidence about scalability of quantum methods.
#limitation:qubit-count — VQE experiments are limited to ~12 active qubits; larger problem instances require clustering, decomposition, or hybrid methods.
#limitation:data-encoding — Fixed-point binary encoding (N * Nt * Nq) inflates QUBO size; clustering/preprocessing is required to make problems tractable for QPUs.
#limitation:noise — Circuit depth (e.g., ~82 CNOTs) and NISQ noise constrain VQE performance on IBM-Q, limiting solution quality for larger instances.
contradictions: The paper shows D-Wave Hybrid and a classical Tensor Network both handle the largest problem sizes (up to Ntot=1272), which contradicts any straightforward claim that quantum methods (annealing) unambiguously outperform classical/quantum-inspired methods on this portfolio task.

The paper demonstrates that VQE on IBM-Q is limited to very small clustered instances (~12 qubits) and does not scale, contradicting optimistic narratives that NISQ variational algorithms will soon scale to realistic portfolio sizes without hybrid decomposition or classical assistance.
